Miquel

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: three circles drawn through a triangle's corners always meet at one point.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B and C, or slide the three marked points along the sides. Press “Line up the points” to see what happens when the three marked points lie on one straight line.
Look for the math

Drag a corner or a marked point and the three circles change shape, but they keep one point in common. Put the three marked points on one straight line and something else joins them there.

One point for three circles

Let the triangle be A, B, C and put X on the side BC, Y on CA and Z on AB. The circle through A, Y and Z, the one through B, X and Z, and the one through C, X and Y all pass through a second shared point P. This is the pivot theorem, the simplest form of Miquel's theorem. The marked points may sit beyond a corner, on the extension of a side: the circles still meet.

When the three points line up

Now make X, Y and Z lie on one line, a fourth line crossing the triangle. The complete quadrilateral they form has four triangles, and the four circles through each triangle all pass through the same P. In particular, the circumcircle of ABC (red here) passes through P. The orange straight line is the marked line; the old page calls it a simson line of P with respect to the triangles.

How the old page proves it

Take two of the four triangles, say 123 and 124. Their circles meet at P. The feet of the perpendiculars from P to the sides of triangle 123 lie on one simson line, and so do the feet for triangle 124. These two lines share two feet, so they are the same line. That forces the feet for the other two triangles onto it too, which puts P on their circles. Four circles, one point.

What the checks found and what changed

The logic test tries hundreds of triangles, with side points both on the sides and on their extensions. The pivot claim and the four-circle claim both hold to about a millionth; sliding one marked point off the line makes the circumcircle leave P. The live cut-the-knot page still gives the words but no longer embeds the Java applet; its 28 September 2006 Wayback copy shows <applet code="Miquel" width="480" height="300">, and that is the applet ported here. This is not the sibling applet MiquelTheoremForCircles, which starts with two triples of points and proves an extra circle-concurrency claim using inversion; this one starts with a triangle and a point on each side line. The two buttons are new: the original had only mouse dragging and a hint printed on the canvas. Draggable dots also stop a little short of the SVG edge so they stay visible and easy to press on a phone.

Try dragging a marked point past a corner onto the extension of its side: the three circles still meet at P.
